page: Google Cloud Platform c4-highmem-288-metal is a bare-metal server instance architected for memory-intensive enterprise tasks and dense multi-threaded computation. Built on the x86_64 architecture, it is powered by an Intel Xeon 6985P-C processor clocked at 4.2 GHz. The hardware layout features 144 physical cores running two threads per core, providing 288 dedicated vCPUs. Cache allocation includes 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and a massive 504 MB L3 cache pool. The CPU instruction set integrates advanced acceleration vector and matrix engines, including AVX-512, AMX Tile, and AMX INT8, along with hardware-level cryptographic extensions like AES-NI and VAES.

The system is equipped with 2232.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 6 GHz, yielding approximately 7.75 GB of RAM per vCPU. This configuration provides uncached large-block read bandwidth of 1090.07 GB/sec and write bandwidth of 412.54 GB/sec, with cached small-block reads exceeding 23000 GB/sec. The instance includes no bundled local NVMe storage and contains zero GPUs, meaning persistent data storage and graphic acceleration depend entirely on network-attached infrastructure.

Benchmark results validate exceptional multi-threaded performance, with top-tier rankings in multi-core stress-ng (313057.86), multi-threaded bzip3 decompression (1752.0 GB/sec), and PassMark CPU scoring (179028.27). In-memory database workloads demonstrate extreme throughput, posting 423.02 million Redis SET operations per second and leading PassMark database operations scores. While single-core execution sits in the average tier, the server handles large-scale CPU-based LLM prompt processing proficiently due to AMX instruction support, though autoregressive token generation remains limited compared to dedicated GPU nodes.

The c4-highmem-288-metal offers cost efficiency at the absolute upper tier of bare-metal resource density by removing virtualization overhead. It is best suited for enterprise in-memory databases, large-scale Redis caching tiers, memory-bound high-performance computing (HPC), and heavy parallel compilation pipelines.
